questions.prompt: Stream A has missing earlier bytes in an HTTP/2 TCP connection; later stream B bytes have arrived. Which boundary remains?

options.label: HTTP/2 interleaves streams, but missing TCP bytes can stall delivery across them.
HTTP/2 lets TCP deliver B around every missing byte.
Only the number of browser connections determines this stall.

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 interleaves application exchanges, but TCP still delivers one ordered byte stream. Stream IDs cannot remove the transport gap; connection-count limits are a different constraint.

questions.prompt: Which statement keeps HTTP/3, QUIC and UDP contracts distinct?

options.label: HTTP/3 uses UDP and therefore has no reliability mechanism.
QUIC is the name of an HTTP/2 TCP frame.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP; QUIC supplies reliable ordered stream delivery.

questions.explanation: HTTP/3 maps onto QUIC, which carries its stream/recovery mechanisms over UDP. The lower datagram protocol alone does not establish the application delivery promise.

questions.prompt: QUIC stream A lacks bytes while B has all its required bytes. What is a justified claim?

options.label: Every stream must always wait for every loss on A.
Another QUIC stream may progress, while shared congestion and compression dependencies still matter.
B has unlimited independent bandwidth and no other dependencies.

questions.explanation: Per-stream ordered delivery can let B progress without A's missing data. Connection congestion, flow-control budgets, application dependencies and compression can still constrain progress.

questions.prompt: An Ethernet/IPv4 LAN frame is sent to a router on the way to a remote service. What does its link destination identify?

options.label: A link address identifies the local next hop; it is not the remote application's identity.
The remote user account and application authorization.
One permanent end-to-end MAC address for the entire Internet route.

questions.explanation: In this LAN fixture, routing selects a next hop and ARP resolves its local Ethernet address. That address is separate from the remote server identity, TLS authority and resource permission.

questions.prompt: A small VPN README reports success where only TCP ports are available. How should you use that evidence?

options.label: Treat every workload as faster, anonymous and independently audited.
Assume a VPN removes every inner and outer recovery queue.
The author reports a TCP-restricted use case; verify the tunnel and inner/outer loss tradeoff for your workload.

questions.explanation: The author's use case motivates a selected transport review. It is not an independent cryptographic audit or universal benchmark; verify both recovery loops and deployment requirements.
